en.title: Jess Lourey Revisits a Notorious Killer, But With a Crucial Twist
en.summary: Author Jess Lourey delves into the dark history of serial killer Paul Michael Stephani, known as the 'Weepy-Voiced Killer.' Her latest novel, 'The Crying Killer,' dares to shift the narrative focus away from the perpetrator and onto the lives of those he impacted.
en.body:
Serial killings often hold a disproportionate sway over the public imagination, even as they represent a small fraction of overall homicides. This fascination is a complex phenomenon, fueled by a desire for self-protection, the primal thrill of a scary story told from a safe distance, and the sheer volume of such crimes in certain regions. The United States, in particular, has a staggering number of documented serial killers compared to other nations, making the subject an unavoidable part of the national consciousness.

Minnesota, home to author **Jess Lourey**, has certainly seen its share of disturbing cases. One of the most notorious is **Paul Michael Stephani**, infamously dubbed the 'Weepy-Voiced Killer' for his distinctive, whining phone calls to authorities made after most of his brutal crimes. Stephani's story, marked by a difficult childhood and a string of violent acts in the Minneapolis/Saint Paul area, has long been a grim chapter in the region's history.

## Shifting the Narrative Spotlight

**Jess Lourey**'s latest novel, **The Crying Killer**, takes inspiration from Stephani's horrific crimes but makes a deliberate and powerful choice: to redirect the reader's attention. Instead of rehashing the killer's pathology or dwelling on the gruesome details of his methods, Lourey focuses intensely on the victims. This approach offers a profound re-examination of true crime narratives, seeking to honor the lives lost and the individuals whose stories were tragically cut short.

> "My latest thriller, The Crying Killer, is inspired by Paul Michael Stephani, an American serial killer active in the Minneapolis/Saint Paul area" — Jess Lourey

This deliberate shift is crucial. It moves beyond the sensationalism that often surrounds serial killer narratives and instead emphasizes the human cost of such violence. By concentrating on the lives, dreams, and experiences of those affected, **The Crying Killer** aims to provide a more empathetic and complete picture, reminding readers that behind every statistic is a person whose absence leaves an irreplaceable void.

## A New Perspective for True Crime Aficionados

For readers who are drawn to the darker corners of storytelling, **Jess Lourey**'s work in **The Crying Killer** offers a compelling reason to engage with the genre anew. The true crime community is constantly seeking deeper understanding and more meaningful connections to the stories being told. Lourey's decision to prioritize the victims' perspectives taps into this desire, potentially offering a cathartic and illuminating experience for those who have followed similar cases or simply appreciate stories told with a strong ethical compass.

This novel is not just another retelling of a killer's spree; it's an invitation to consider the ripple effects of violence and the enduring power of individual lives. It challenges the typical narrative structure of true crime, asking readers to look beyond the monster and see the humanity that was extinguished.

## What's Next

**The Crying Killer** was published in 2026, and **Jess Lourey** continues to explore complex themes in her writing. Readers eager to experience this unique take on a notorious case can seek out the novel wherever books are sold.

content_raw: Serial killings have an outsize grip on the American imagination despite accounting for only one percent of homicides. Millions of us tune into podcasts like Crime Junkie and Morbid, binge documentaries like Conversations with a Killer: The Ted Bundy Tapes, devour books like Michelle McNamara’s I’ll Be Gone in the Dark. I think there’s an element of self-protection to the obsession. If we learn how the predators hunt, we might be able to keep ourselves safe. Plus, there’s the timeless appeal of hearing a scary story while you yourself are safe. But those factors are universal, so I don’t think they account for the uniquely American fascination with serial killers. That, I think, is explained by ratios. Specifically, the U.S. has more documented serial killers than any other nation, over twenty times as many as England, which ranks second. If a population has a twentyfold difference in anything deadly—car accidents, earthquakes, salmonella outbreaks—it’s going to rightfully invite attention. On a per capita basis, the three states that consistently top the list for numbers of serial killings are Alaska, Montana, and Nevada, though my home state of Minnesota has recorded its share of repeat offenders. Paul Michael Stephani, otherwise known as the Weepy-Voiced Killer, is one of the most notorious. He earned his nickname due to his whining, anonymous phone calls to police after all but one of his gruesome crimes. Stephani was born September 8, 1944, in Austin, Minnesota, to a devoutly Catholic mother. His father died when he was young, and his mother remarried a man who was reportedly abusive. Stephani, now part of a blended family of ten children, moved out of the house and to Saint Paul in the mid-’60s. There he held various low-wage jobs, including as a shipping clerk and janitor. He stayed mostly below the radar until December 31, 1980, when he viciously attacked twenty-year-old Karen Potack, beating her with a tire iron and leaving her for dead. In a span of two years, he would go on to murder three women and stab a fourth who—like Karen Potack—survived, bringing his total number of known victims to five. Because of his childhood spent in a deeply religious family, it’s possible that Stephani’s high-pitched confessional calls after his attacks were not just theatrics but attempts at atonement, pathetic pleas for absolution that offered no comfort to his victims or their families. (For example, he complained, “I’ll never make it into heaven!” when admitting to stabbing Barbara Simons, a nurse, over forty times. As with his other weeping phone calls, he left no identifying information.) His recorded confessions brought him wide attention, which in turn made him seem larger than life. Like many—all?—serial killers Americans find themselves fascinated with, though, the myth of Paul Michael Stephani overshadowed the reality.
